person.name: Ahmed Gameel
person.title: Data Engineer
person.headline: Batch and streaming pipelines, on AWS and in the open
person.intro: I ship AWS Glue and PySpark jobs at DigitalH. On the side I built Tower Health Stream, a Kafka and Flink pipeline that watches 10,192 Egyptian cell towers and flags trouble in under 150 ms.
about:
I care about the boring parts that make data trustworthy: contracts at the edges, quality checks before anything is published, and numbers that can be traced back to where they came from.
At DigitalH I build ETL jobs on AWS Glue with PySpark and Python over data in Amazon S3. Outside work I learn by building complete systems end to end: a streaming pipeline with Kafka and Flink, batch pipelines orchestrated with Airflow, and a SQL Server warehouse modeled as a star schema.
I am early in my career and I want to grow in a team that ships reliable, well documented data.

highlights: Design and develop ETL and ELT pipelines using AWS Glue, PySpark and Python.
Build and maintain Glue jobs that ingest, transform and optimize datasets stored in Amazon S3.
Work with the data engineering team to deliver production workflows for enterprise projects.

experience.context: A training program run by Egypt's Ministry of Communications and IT.

Designed and published interactive dashboards and a real world capstone project.
Set up reproducible Hadoop environments with Docker and built warehouse tables with Hive.
Processed data in memory with Spark and automated flows with NiFi across PostgreSQL and MongoDB.

projects.name: Tower Health Stream
projects.summary: A streaming pipeline that watches simulated telemetry from 10,192 real Egyptian cell tower locations.
projects.problem: Telecom teams often learn about a weak tower only after customers complain. I wanted to see how early a streaming pipeline could flag it, and whether it could tell a hardware fault from bad weather.
projects.built: Kafka carries tower events. One Flink job validates them and routes bad records to a dead letter queue, a second classifies anomalies and rolls them up per area in 10 minute tumbling windows. A Python service adds live weather to each alert, Iceberg keeps the history, and Grafana shows it all. Airflow and dbt on DuckDB handle the batch side.
projects.result: On a local Docker stack it kept up with 2,038 events per second and raised alerts in under 150 ms.

decisions.title: Tumbling windows for regional outages
decisions.body: Fixed 10 minute buckets give one clean result per window, so an outage is never double counted and the logic stays deterministic.

decisions.title: A dead letter queue, not a silent drop
decisions.body: Events outside the valid range go to their own topic, so bad data stays visible and can be replayed.

decisions.title: Weather as context
decisions.body: Every alert is enriched with live Open-Meteo weather, so the team can tell a hardware fault from a storm and respond differently.

decisions.title: Kafka in KRaft mode
decisions.body: No ZooKeeper to run, one less moving part in a local stack that already has eight services.

next: Move the Python sinks into Flink so delivery to PostgreSQL is checkpointed.
Add a schema registry so a producer change cannot break consumers.
Run it on managed services with infrastructure as code.

projects.name: Log Analytics ETL
projects.summary: An Airflow and PySpark pipeline that turns 3.5 GB of raw web server logs into clean Parquet and reports.
projects.problem: Raw access logs are slow to query and expensive to keep as text. The questions people ask of them (who is hitting us, what fails, how much is bots) need structure first.
projects.built: Airflow DAGs split the log by date, parse each day with PySpark, join hostnames from a 258K row lookup, apply quality rules and write daily analytics reports. New files are picked up automatically.
projects.result: 10.36 million records processed end to end in about 5 minutes, and Parquet cut the data from 3.5 GB to 235 MB.

decisions.title: Split by date first
decisions.body: Daily files let Spark parse days independently and let Airflow pick up a new day as soon as it lands.

decisions.title: Columnar storage early
decisions.body: Writing Parquet right after parsing means every later stage reads 93% less data.

decisions.title: Quality as its own stage
decisions.body: Duplicates, malformed IPs, invalid status codes and nulls are handled in one DAG, so analytics only reads clean data.

next: Unit tests for the log parser with real sample lines.
Incremental runs driven by data intervals instead of folder polling.
Publish the daily reports as a small dashboard.

projects.name: Unified Sales Warehouse
projects.summary: A SQL Server warehouse that combines CRM and ERP sales data into one star schema.
projects.problem: Sales data lived in two systems with different keys and formats for the same customers and products.
projects.built: SSIS loads six raw source tables into a Bronze layer, stored procedures clean and standardize them in Silver, and Gold exposes a star schema with fact_sales, dim_customers and dim_products as views.
projects.result: One consistent model for sales reporting, where each number can be traced back a layer at a time.

decisions.title: Medallion layers
decisions.body: Bronze keeps files as they arrived, Silver applies the business rules, Gold is what analysts query.

decisions.title: Gold as views
decisions.body: The star schema is views over Silver, so a model change needs no reload.

decisions.title: Full reload in Silver
decisions.body: TRUNCATE and INSERT keeps the procedures simple at this size. Incremental loads are the next step.

next: Slowly changing dimensions for customer history.
Data tests on keys and row counts between layers.
